newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss private bank says it has no Jewish assets.
newsitem.headline: Swiss private bank says it has no Jewish assets.

text.p: Switzerland's leading private bank Pictet & Cie, which will be among the first Swiss banks investigated by auditors hunting the money of Jews killed by Hitler, said on Thursday that it had found no trace of such assets.

"We made a brief review of our existing archives and we did not find anything," Sylvain Matthey, head of the bank's legal office, told reporters during a news conference by Paul Volcker, head of a joint commission investigating dormant accounts.

Switzerland is under fire from Jewish groups who charge that its banks profitted blatantly from millions, perhaps billions, of dollars of dormant assets of Holocaust victims and acted as a clearing house for looted Nazi gold.
Matthey said Pictet's search also covered dormant safe deposit boxes but found no dormant Jewish assets dating from World War Two and its aftermath.
Volcker's commission, the Independent Committee of Eminent Persons, is overseeing an audit of banks and aims to return any money it discovers to Holocaust survivors or heirs of the victims.
In addition to Pictet, it has named four other banks, Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corporation, Spar and Leihkasse Berne and Bank Cantonale Vaudoise, for its pilot project.

Volcker said the five were selected because they were representative of Swiss banks and not because of any suspicion that they might be holding Jewish assets. An investigation of more Swiss banks would begin after a committe reviewed the pilot results in September.

Private banks in Switzerland, a top centre for managing the wealth of the world's super-rich, are notoriously secretive and many Geneva financiers feel uneasy at the prospect of their names being in the news.

But Matthey said Pictet, the first in Geneva's opaque private banking community to come under the spotlight, felt confident that the audit would not make its clients nervous and violate banking secrecy laws.
"This audit has to be viewed in its historical context. It's exceptional. We don't think you can attach a value af precedence to it. It is uniquely about the wartime period," he said.
"We do not think our clients will object to this procedure. To the contrary, I believe our clients will be very glad to know that their bank was managed by people with ethics and morality."
Asked if the audit might find dormant Jewish wealth in Geneva, he said: "I cannot speak for other banks but it is not excluded. Geneva is a traditionally important financial centre."
